Every survey taken after a navigation with install:true. 540 dims graded. This is the device/language pair of the English desktop walk banked in the same session, and it found what only a Filipino walk could.

THE FRONT DOOR WAS IN ENGLISH FOR A FILIPINO READER, AND THE TRANSLATION WAS SITTING RIGHT THERE. With wh_lang='fil' and html lang='fil', index rendered 50 of its 56 data-i keys in ENGLISH - "What is WorkHive?", "Install WorkHive", "Today at a Glance", "Free Industrial Tools for Every Filipino Worker" - while _ohFIL, the page's own dictionary, held 58 keys with a Filipino string for every one of them ("Ano ang WorkHive?", "I-install ang WorkHive", "Ngayong Araw sa Isang Tingin"). Nothing was missing and nothing was mistranslated. It simply was never applied.

TWO FAULTS, THE SECOND HIDDEN BEHIND THE FIRST.
(1) THE STORED LOCALE WAS NEVER APPLIED AT BOOT. WH_LANG is read from localStorage on load, so _t()-rendered strings came out Filipino - which is exactly why the page LOOKED bilingual in places and why this survived: "Mag-sign In" and "Higit pa" render through _t(), so a glance suggested the swap was working. But setLang(), which is what applies the dictionary to the static [data-i] markup, was only ever called from the EN/FIL toggle's CLICK handler. A reader who chose Filipino on a previous visit came back to an English front door, every time. Same defect hive.html carried and had fixed earlier the same day (it read a hardcoded 'en' rather than the stored value); this is the landing page's half of it, and it went unnoticed because index is the one page nobody signs in to first.
(2) THE SWAP RAN ONCE, OVER A PAGE HALF OF WHICH DID NOT EXIST YET. setLang snapshotted document.querySelectorAll('[data-i]') and translated exactly that set, so markup rendered LATER kept English permanently: the ops-home panel (#ops-home - "Today at a Glance", "Quick Actions"), the account menu (#user-menu - "Sign out", "Deactivate account", "Change Password") and the PWA install button, all of which paint after auth and data resolve. Proven rather than reasoned: calling setLang('fil') a second time from the console, after everything had painted, flipped all five to Filipino immediately.

FIXED, BOTH HALVES, IN index.html. The dictionary application became _ohApplyI18n(root), which can translate any subtree; a MutationObserver (re-entrancy guarded) runs it on nodes added while FIL is active, so late renders no longer need every renderer to remember; and the stored locale is now applied at boot on DOMContentLoaded. _ohEnCap captures a key's English the FIRST time that key is seen rather than only during the initial sweep, so switching back to English restores late markup too.

MEASURED AFTER, INCLUDING THE DIRECTION THAT COULD HAVE BEEN BROKEN. Filipino: 0 of 56 keys still showing their English capture (from 50), page text grew 252,226 -> 256,271 characters as the longer Filipino strings landed. English round-trip: setLang('en') restores "What is WorkHive?", "Install WorkHive", "Today at a Glance" - including the late-rendered keys, which is the proof the first-seen capture works - and setLang('fil') returns them. An i18n fix that quietly broke English readers would have been a worse defect than the one it fixed.

A DATA ERROR CAUGHT BEFORE BANKING, worth recording because it would have been invisible afterwards: the first hive survey in this walk was actually INDEX. The post-sign-in redirect did not land on hive.html and the fallback did not fire, so the file called hive.json carried index's dims - the same "SMRP world-class benchmarks" and "bigSizes=[67,36,30,20]" readings, and 256,289 characters against index's 256,271. Every survey in this walk now records its own href and title so the next one cannot make the same mistake silently.

J1's onboarding, walked IN FILIPINO: index -> hive -> asset-hub -> logbook -> pm-scheduler -> alert-hub, phone-390 mobile+touch, as Romeo Beltran with wh_lang=fil, through the chrome-devtools MCP. THIS WALK FOUND MORE IN THE RULER THAN IN THE PAGES, and both halves are worth recording. THE PRODUCT DEFECT, on the page a worker opens most: hive.html threw a Filipino worker's language away three separate ways - it hardcoded window.WH_LANG='en' in an inline script that runs BEFORE utils.js (so it actively suppressed the platform's own locale floor, and localStorage saying 'fil' rendered ZERO Filipino tokens); setLang never PERSISTED the choice, making it the only one of four toggle-bearing pages that neither read nor saved it; and reading the preference is not applying it, so the ~92 static data-i labels needed the swap run once on load or the board would MEASURE better while the person still read 'YOUR OPEN WORK'. The worker's own card was the last holdout: no data-i on either static label, and of its four JS strings only the ERROR path went through _t() - so the one message a Filipino technician was guaranteed to understand was the failure. All fixed and verified live: 0 -> 34 Filipino tokens, the card now reading 'BUKAS MONG TRABAHO / 4 trabahong nakatalaga sa iyo / I-tap para tingnan at i-update ang mga ito sa logbook mo. / Buksan ang Logbook'. THE INSTRUMENT DEFECT, which was larger: dim X1 failed on ALL SIX Filipino surfaces (index 0%, asset-hub 38%, alert-hub 67%, hive/logbook/pm-scheduler 80%) where the ENGLISH walk of the same pages failed none - because its guidance vocabulary was English-only on a bilingual product. 'Wala pang nakuwentang Weibull fit. Pindutin...' says PRESS; 'Walang tool na tumugma sa paghahanap' is word-for-word 'No tool matched the search', which passes in English via the match term; 'lalabas dito ang score' is 'a score will appear here', which passes via will-appear. Three groups of Filipino twins were added - action verbs, filter/search terms and reassurance phrases - all MEASURED from the 491 _t(en,fil) strings the platform itself ships (Subukan 119, Buksan 13, Tingnan 7, Pindutin 6, Punan 5), never invented. asset-hub X1 now grades 100% in BOTH languages, and this journey went from fourteen sub-100 dims to seven. Every one of the 62 pending Filipino walks would otherwise have banked the same false dead-ends. Surveyed: alert-hub 90 dims, 1 sub-100 | asset-hub 90 dims, 1 sub-100 | hive 90 dims, 3 sub-100 | index 90 dims, 0 sub-100 | logbook 90 dims, 2 sub-100 | pm-scheduler 90 dims, 0 sub-100. [2026-09-10] RETRACTED and REMOVED (the measurement itself is false): B3 - "asset-hub: B3 67% - sentences=3 · >20w=0 · passive=0 · grade>8=1". B3's readability grade is Flesch-Kincaid, whose coefficients are fitted to ENGLISH, and it was applied unchanged to Filipino prose. Measured on the platform's OWN parallel corpus (i18n/*.json holds each English string beside its shipped Filipino): across 193 sentence pairs of 8+ words, the Filipino grades HARDER in 180 of them (93%), mean +4.53 grades, median +4.65; syllables-per-word 1.51 EN vs 1.82 FIL; mean grade 8.7 EN vs 13.3 FIL. 64 pairs PASS in English and FAIL in Filipino, only 2 the other way. The clearest case: "Pick the closest match. You can change scope later." grades 2.3, and its faithful, plain translation "Piliin ang pinakamalapit. Puwede mong baguhin ang scope mamaya." grades 14.1 - the same sentence, +11.8 grades, for being Filipino. Tagalog is agglutinative (naitatala, nagpapalago, disiplinang), so its syllables-per-word runs structurally higher and FK's 11.8 syllable term dominates. These findings measured the LANGUAGE, not the copy, and the platform was being penalised for translating well. The ruler is fixed: Filipino prose is now exempt from GRADE, never from length or voice - the same rule this rubric already applies to standards vocabulary. Only findings that rest ENTIRELY on the grade are withdrawn (no long sentence, no passive voice); English B3 findings stand, because FK is valid for English, and every Filipino finding that also carried a >20-word or passive offence stands on that evidence.

This is the device/language pair of the English desktop walk banked in the same session, and it found what only a Filipino walk could.

THE FRONT DOOR WAS IN ENGLISH FOR A FILIPINO READER, AND THE TRANSLATION WAS SITTING RIGHT THERE. With wh_lang='fil' and html lang='fil', index rendered 50 of its 56 data-i keys in ENGLISH - "What is WorkHive?", "Install WorkHive", "Today at a Glance", "Free Industrial Tools for Every Filipino Worker" - while _ohFIL, the page's own dictionary, held 58 keys with a Filipino string for every one of them ("Ano ang WorkHive?", "I-install ang WorkHive", "Ngayong Araw sa Isang Tingin"). Nothing was missing and nothing was mistranslated. It simply was never applied.

TWO FAULTS, THE SECOND HIDDEN BEHIND THE FIRST.
(1) THE STORED LOCALE WAS NEVER APPLIED AT BOOT. WH_LANG is read from localStorage on load, so _t()-rendered strings came out Filipino - which is exactly why the page LOOKED bilingual in places and why this survived: "Mag-sign In" and "Higit pa" render through _t(), so a glance suggested the swap was working. But setLang(), which is what applies the dictionary to the static [data-i] markup, was only ever called from the EN/FIL toggle's CLICK handler. A reader who chose Filipino on a previous visit came back to an English front door, every time. Same defect hive.html carried and had fixed earlier the same day (it read a hardcoded 'en' rather than the stored value); this is the landing page's half of it, and it went unnoticed because index is the one page nobody signs in to first.
(2) THE SWAP RAN ONCE, OVER A PAGE HALF OF WHICH DID NOT EXIST YET. setLang snapshotted document.querySelectorAll('[data-i]') and translated exactly that set, so markup rendered LATER kept English permanently: the ops-home panel (#ops-home - "Today at a Glance", "Quick Actions"), the account menu (#user-menu - "Sign out", "Deactivate account", "Change Password") and the PWA install button, all of which paint after auth and data resolve. Proven rather than reasoned: calling setLang('fil') a second time from the console, after everything had painted, flipped all five to Filipino immediately.

FIXED, BOTH HALVES, IN index.html. The dictionary application became _ohApplyI18n(root), which can translate any subtree; a MutationObserver (re-entrancy guarded) runs it on nodes added while FIL is active, so late renders no longer need every renderer to remember; and the stored locale is now applied at boot on DOMContentLoaded. _ohEnCap captures a key's English the FIRST time that key is seen rather than only during the initial sweep, so switching back to English restores late markup too.

Filipino: 0 of 56 keys still showing their English capture (from 50), page text grew 252,226 -> 256,271 characters as the longer Filipino strings landed. English round-trip: setLang('en') restores "What is WorkHive?", "Install WorkHive", "Today at a Glance" - including the late-rendered keys, which is the proof the first-seen capture works - and setLang('fil') returns them. J1 ONBOARDING IN FILIPINO on desktop-1280: index -> hive -> asset-hub -> logbook -> pm-scheduler -> alert-hub, wh_lang='fil', normal conditions, present moment, viewport 1280x900 with mobile/touch emulation OFF. index walked SIGNED OUT (the front door), then in through the platform's own wall, then the member surfaces as Rosa dela Cruz of Dela Cruz Delivery Fleet. Every survey taken after a navigation with install:true. 540 dims graded. This is the device/language pair of the English desktop walk banked in the same session, and it found what only a Filipino walk could.

THE FRONT DOOR WAS IN ENGLISH FOR A FILIPINO READER, AND THE TRANSLATION WAS SITTING RIGHT THERE. With wh_lang='fil' and html lang='fil', index rendered 50 of its 56 data-i keys in ENGLISH - "What is WorkHive?", "Install WorkHive", "Today at a Glance", "Free Industrial Tools for Every Filipino Worker" - while _ohFIL, the page's own dictionary, held 58 keys with a Filipino string for every one of them ("Ano ang WorkHive?", "I-install ang WorkHive", "Ngayong Araw sa Isang Tingin"). Nothing was missing and nothing was mistranslated. It simply was never applied.

TWO FAULTS, THE SECOND HIDDEN BEHIND THE FIRST.
(1) THE STORED LOCALE WAS NEVER APPLIED AT BOOT. WH_LANG is read from localStorage on load, so _t()-rendered strings came out Filipino - which is exactly why the page LOOKED bilingual in places and why this survived: "Mag-sign In" and "Higit pa" render through _t(), so a glance suggested the swap was working. But setLang(), which is what applies the dictionary to the static [data-i] markup, was only ever called from the EN/FIL toggle's CLICK handler. A reader who chose Filipino on a previous visit came back to an English front door, every time. Same defect hive.html carried and had fixed earlier the same day (it read a hardcoded 'en' rather than the stored value); this is the landing page's half of it, and it went unnoticed because index is the one page nobody signs in to first.
(2) THE SWAP RAN ONCE, OVER A PAGE HALF OF WHICH DID NOT EXIST YET. setLang snapshotted document.querySelectorAll('[data-i]') and translated exactly that set, so markup rendered LATER kept English permanently: the ops-home panel (#ops-home - "Today at a Glance", "Quick Actions"), the account menu (#user-menu - "Sign out", "Deactivate account", "Change Password") and the PWA install button, all of which paint after auth and data resolve. Proven rather than reasoned: calling setLang('fil') a second time from the console, after everything had painted, flipped all five to Filipino immediately.

FIXED, BOTH HALVES, IN index.html. The dictionary application became _ohApplyI18n(root), which can translate any subtree; a MutationObserver (re-entrancy guarded) runs it on nodes added while FIL is active, so late renders no longer need every renderer to remember; and the stored locale is now applied at boot on DOMContentLoaded. _ohEnCap captures a key's English the FIRST time that key is seen rather than only during the initial sweep, so switching back to English restores late markup too.

Filipino: 0 of 56 keys still showing their English capture (from 50), page text grew 252,226 -> 256,271 characters as the longer Filipino strings landed. English round-trip: setLang('en') restores "What is WorkHive?", "Install WorkHive", "Today at a Glance" - including the late-rendered keys, which is the proof the first-seen capture works - and setLang('fil') returns them. An i18n fix that quietly broke English readers would have been a worse defect than the one it fixed.

THE FINDING, AND IT WAS THE PARTIAL-FIX SHAPE INSIDE THE VERY TABLE THAT DOCUMENTS THE RULE. achievements graded C2 99%: the hero tier chip "Silver Technician" measured 4.13:1 against the 4.5:1 that 11px text owes. The first fix attempt was WRONG and the re-measurement caught it - `.standing-rank.silver { color: #94A3B8 }` in achievements.html is the same value at 0.7rem, but it is not the element that renders the chip, and C2 came back unchanged at 4.13:1. The chip is #hero-tier-label, coloured INLINE by JS from a shared constant: ACHIEVEMENT_TIERS in utils.js. That table carries its own comment - "tier.color is used as small TEXT ('Iron Technician' chip) as well as ring/tint - each value must clear WCAG AA 4.5:1 on the dark tints. Iron #7B8794 measured 3.08 and Bronze #CD7F32 2.6-3.3 as text (2026-07-16); lightened same-hue." Iron and Bronze were lightened for exactly this rule in July. Silver was left at its original value and has been failing ever since, in the table whose comment states the requirement.

FIXED AT THE SOURCE, the same move the July fix made: Silver lightened same-hue to slate-300 (#CBD5E1) in ACHIEVEMENT_TIERS, so it reaches every surface that renders a Silver tier rather than the one page that was walked, and the achievements.html `.standing-rank.silver` rule was brought to the same value so one tier has one colour. Verified live: the chip renders rgb(203,213,225), achievements C2 reports ZERO offenders and the page reads 100%. Component purity still 19/19 (slate is not a brand literal).

Each page surveyed only after its own text length held steady across three consecutive reads, so no page is graded mid-render.

THE FIND IS THAT THE PERMISSION WALL ONLY SPOKE ENGLISH, AND IT PUNISHED THE PRODUCT FOR REFUSING CORRECTLY IN FILIPINO. audit-log scored E3 0% "NO source chip", G1 0% "no status region", I2 0% "no reserved/optimistic block" - three zeroes against a page that was doing exactly the right thing: a worker is not a supervisor, so the page shows him an honest locked card instead of the log. The rubric already knew to excuse that state and keys it on the MECHANISM - a visible .gate-card / [id^=gate-] - which audit-log ships correctly as <div id="gate-not-supervisor" class="gate-card">, and which the probe confirmed visible. What failed was the second half of the test: the gate's TEXT had to match permission vocabulary, and that vocabulary was English-only. Under FIL the card reads "Para sa supervisor lang", which matches nothing in /supervisors? only|admins? only|.../, so the wall went undetected. The bias is one-directional and precise: the identical page in English is excused and the Filipino one is marked broken. An oracle's vocabulary is part of the oracle - the same wound as the founder-console probe that missed #no-access-gate by knowing only one spelling of the mechanism.

FIXED AND EVIDENCED IN THREE STATES, and the Filipino side is MEASURED, never guessed: "Para sa supervisor lang", "Supervisor lang", "Miyembro ng hive lang", "Sumali (muna) sa hive" and "Para lang sa mga platform admin" are what i18n/*.json actually ships; the platform has no "walang access" string today, and when it gains one the pattern must grow with it. Deliberately NOT a blanket match on "lang", which is an ordinary Filipino word - the match is anchored to a permission noun, and the whole test still runs only inside a VISIBLE gate card, so the structure bounds the risk. Verified live: FIL audit-log now returns E3/G1/I2 as N/A with the permission-wall reason and the page reads 98% (was 93%); EN audit-log still detects its "Supervisors only" card and excuses the same three; and logbook, which has zero gate cards, still MEASURES all three at 100% rather than being quietly excused. A ruler that excuses too much is the same defect as one that punishes too much.

NO STALE FINDINGS FROM THE RULER CHANGE, checked rather than assumed - and my first check was wrong. Findings carry `evidence`, not a `pct`, so an initial query keyed on pct returned a clean zero that meant nothing. Re-run against the evidence text, 765 banked findings carry the wall signature; 75 sit on walks that include a gated page, 12 of those are Filipino, and every one of the 12 names a page that has no wall for this persona (index, and an RA-11285 learn checklist) rather than the gated page in the path. Measured across the dictionaries: 44 English strings carry a freshness word, 25 keep it in Filipino by loanword (snapshot, refresh, generate survive translation) and 19 do not, and those 19 were unreadable to this dim. The ruler is fixed with exactly those measured forms - kalkula/kuwenta (the two verbs Filipino uses for compute), binubuo (built), hiniling (on demand), nakalipas (ago), and the na-/nire- prefixed loanwords the English stems miss because the pattern demands the -d participle. rows.clean_note:
One in-motion MCP walk, banked onto 6 row(s) that share its cell, page path, language, condition and moment (they differ only in which hive's data sits behind the screens - see tools/critic_walk_groups.py). W3237/W3240/W3243/W3246/W3249/W3252 — the AI-assisted day, walked by a WORKER in FILIPINO on phone-390: assistant -> voice-journal -> logbook -> audit-log -> analytics. bryangarcia@auth.workhiveph.com, hive Baguio Textile Mills, wh_hive_role=worker, wh_lang=fil, viewport receipt 390x845 CSS on every survey. assistant and voice-journal had never been walked in Filipino in this program. 450 dims graded, 7 sub-100. Each page surveyed only after its own text length held steady across three consecutive reads, so no page is graded mid-render.

THE FIND IS THAT THE PERMISSION WALL ONLY SPOKE ENGLISH, AND IT PUNISHED THE PRODUCT FOR REFUSING CORRECTLY IN FILIPINO. audit-log scored E3 0% "NO source chip", G1 0% "no status region", I2 0% "no reserved/optimistic block" - three zeroes against a page that was doing exactly the right thing: a worker is not a supervisor, so the page shows him an honest locked card instead of the log. The rubric already knew to excuse that state and keys it on the MECHANISM - a visible .gate-card / [id^=gate-] - which audit-log ships correctly as <div id="gate-not-supervisor" class="gate-card">, and which the probe confirmed visible. What failed was the second half of the test: the gate's TEXT had to match permission vocabulary, and that vocabulary was English-only. Under FIL the card reads "Para sa supervisor lang", which matches nothing in /supervisors? only|admins? only|.../, so the wall went undetected. The bias is one-directional and precise: the identical page in English is excused and the Filipino one is marked broken. An oracle's vocabulary is part of the oracle - the same wound as the founder-console probe that missed #no-access-gate by knowing only one spelling of the mechanism.

FIXED AND EVIDENCED IN THREE STATES, and the Filipino side is MEASURED, never guessed: "Para sa supervisor lang", "Supervisor lang", "Miyembro ng hive lang", "Sumali (muna) sa hive" and "Para lang sa mga platform admin" are what i18n/*.json actually ships; the platform has no "walang access" string today, and when it gains one the pattern must grow with it. Deliberately NOT a blanket match on "lang", which is an ordinary Filipino word - the match is anchored to a permission noun, and the whole test still runs only inside a VISIBLE gate card, so the structure bounds the risk. Verified live: FIL audit-log now returns E3/G1/I2 as N/A with the permission-wall reason and the page reads 98% (was 93%); EN audit-log still detects its "Supervisors only" card and excuses the same three; and logbook, which has zero gate cards, still MEASURES all three at 100% rather than being quietly excused. A ruler that excuses too much is the same defect as one that punishes too much.

NO STALE FINDINGS FROM THE RULER CHANGE, checked rather than assumed - and my first check was wrong. Findings carry `evidence`, not a `pct`, so an initial query keyed on pct returned a clean zero that meant nothing. Re-run against the evidence text, 765 banked findings carry the wall signature; 75 sit on walks that include a gated page, 12 of those are Filipino, and every one of the 12 names a page that has no wall for this persona (index, and an RA-11285 learn checklist) rather than the gated page in the path. So nothing banked was a misgraded Filipino wall, and nothing needs retracting. A zero is only worth reporting once you have shown the query could have found something.

THE SEVEN FINDINGS. audit-log B3 33% is the sharpest: the locked card is four sentences, one of them 21 words and above grade 8, and it is the ONLY thing this persona can read on the page - the refusal is the entire experience, so its prose carries more weight here than anywhere else in the walk. audit-log A1 75% (an h1 and one 26px tier, no CTA) is the same card seen as layout. analytics repeats its known set - E3 50% (a relative freshness chip with no absolute time), B3 67%, R3 67% - and logbook B3 67% over 52 sentences. assistant and voice-journal both read 100% on their first Filipino walk, with 16/16 and 12/12 elements stamped.

The six rows differ only in which hive's data sits behind the same screens; this walk observed Baguio Textile Mills. Surveyed: analytics 90 dims, 4 sub-100 | assistant 90 dims, 0 sub-100 | audit-log 90 dims, 2 sub-100 | logbook 90 dims, 1 sub-100 | voice-journal 90 dims, 0 sub-100. [2026-09-10] RETRACTED and REMOVED (the measurement itself is false): B3 - "analytics: B3 67% - sentences=34 · >20w=0 · passive=0 · grade>8=3". B3's readability grade is Flesch-Kincaid, whose coefficients are fitted to ENGLISH, and it was applied unchanged to Filipino prose. Measured on the platform's OWN parallel corpus (i18n/*.json holds each English string beside its shipped Filipino): across 193 sentence pairs of 8+ words, the Filipino grades HARDER in 180 of them (93%), mean +4.53 grades, median +4.65; syllables-per-word 1.51 EN vs 1.82 FIL; mean grade 8.7 EN vs 13.3 FIL. 64 pairs PASS in English and FAIL in Filipino, only 2 the other way. The clearest case: "Pick the closest match. You can change scope later." grades 2.3, and its faithful, plain translation "Piliin ang pinakamalapit. Puwede mong baguhin ang scope mamaya." grades 14.1 - the same sentence, +11.8 grades, for being Filipino. Tagalog is agglutinative (naitatala, nagpapalago, disiplinang), so its syllables-per-word runs structurally higher and FK's 11.8 syllable term dominates. These findings measured the LANGUAGE, not the copy, and the platform was being penalised for translating well. The ruler is fixed: Filipino prose is now exempt from GRADE, never from length or voice - the same rule this rubric already applies to standards vocabulary. Only findings that rest ENTIRELY on the grade are withdrawn (no long sentence, no passive voice); English B3 findings stand, because FK is valid for English, and every Filipino finding that also carried a >20-word or passive offence stands on that evidence. [2026-09-10] RETRACTED and REMOVED (the measurement itself is false): E3 - "analytics: E3 50% - chip: "Kakakalkula lang · Batay sa iyong logboo"". E3's freshness vocabulary was ENGLISH-ONLY, so a Filipino page that states its freshness plainly was scored as if it had not. Proven on one page in two languages: analytics reads E3 100% in English on "Saved snapshot, computed 6 min ago · Refresh to recompute" and read 50% in Filipino on "Kakakalkula lang", which is the platform's own shipped translation of "Recomputed just now" - the SAME freshness claim, invisible because the pattern only spoke English. Measured across the dictionaries: 44 English strings carry a freshness word, 25 keep it in Filipino by loanword (snapshot, refresh, generate survive translation) and 19 do not, and those 19 were unreadable to this dim. The ruler is fixed with exactly those measured forms - kalkula/kuwenta (the two verbs Filipino uses for compute), binubuo (built), hiniling (on demand), nakalipas (ago), and the na-/nire- prefixed loanwords the English stems miss because the pattern demands the -d participle. Verified on six cases including the negatives: a chip that names only its SOURCE ("Batay sa iyong logbook", "Based on your logbook") still fails in both languages, so the dim keeps its teeth. Retracted here are ONLY the Filipino findings whose quoted chip the corrected vocabulary now accepts - every one of them a chip that was present and did state its freshness. The Filipino "NO source chip" findings are untouched, because a genuinely missing chip is a real defect in any language, and every English E3 finding stands, because the pattern was always valid for English. This is the fourth English-only vocabulary found in one session, after B3's readability grade, the permission wall and X1's guidance verbs. [2026-09-11] RETRACTED (interpretation only - the measurement stands): R3 - "analytics: R3 67% - cardTreatments=1 · silhouettes=4 for 3 role(s) (pill,8px,bar,0px)". The NUMBER is right and the STORY told about it was wrong. Every note carrying this finding explained it as the four .phase-tab controls falling back to their own 0px corner once the strip wraps at 390. They do not: the parent still has gap:0 and the tabs still have border-radius:0, so R3's joined-group test reads them as ONE BAR at both widths - they were never the fourth silhouette. Re-measured by replicating R3's own roleOf/shapeV against the page root at 390: pill->select(20), 8px->press(12), bar->navigate(4), 0px->press(6). The fourth silhouette is the six .kpi-toggle expanders - Availability, MTBF, MTTR, PM Compliance Rate, Downtime Pareto, Failure Frequency - wearing a square corner while the page's twelve other press controls (refresh-btn, details-toggle, showall-toggle) wear 8px. It is NOT a responsive defect: the toggle is 308px inside a 352px card (87.5%), just under isCardAnatomy's 90% cut-off, and at desktop it crosses that line and is excluded, which is the only reason R3 read 100% at 1280. The inconsistency existed at every width; one width could see it. Fixed by giving .kpi-toggle var(--wh-radius-sm) - the border and tint come from a JS-written inline style that sets no radius, so the class rule wins. Verified at BOTH widths: pill/8px/bar, 3 shapes for 3 roles, 0 collisions, R3 100%, analytics 100%. A mechanism must be measured, not inferred from the one thing that visibly changed.

THE POINT OF THIS WALK WAS TO SECOND-SOURCE THE i18n CLOBBER FIX, AND IT DID. The founder-console find was a single page: whI18nApply's re-apply overwrote every [data-i] element, including those the application had since computed, so a finished value reverted to its placeholder. The fix stamps what the swap wrote (data-i-applied) and skips any element that no longer holds it. hive.html carries the same shape - _elseLine computes a pointer sentence into a data-i element - so it is the honest second case. Probed as a sequence on the live element: read immediately, then again 5s later, past the 200ms-debounced re-apply. Both reads are byte-identical ("Naghihintay din ng review mo: 2 na shift briefing sa Alert Hub") and clobbered=false, with 27 elements carrying the stamp on that page. The mechanism that erased founder-console's health verdict is now proven inert on a second page that was never touched to make it so.

The same line also settles the double-pluralisation I introduced and then fixed: it reads "2 na shift briefing", not "2 na shift briefings". Composing each countable phrase whole per language is holding.

THE NINE FINDINGS. B3 is the pattern, not an incident: four of the six pages fail it (analytics 33%, community 67%, shift-brain 67%, hive 67%) on the same axis - sentences above grade 8, 1 to 4 per page, with no long sentences and almost no passive voice. The prose is not rambling, it is polysyllabic, and it is being read here by a fleet supervisor in her second language. analytics is the worst at 33% (30 sentences, 1 above grade 8, 2 passive).

hive G3 0% is the sharpest single number in the walk: 24 controls on the board and 3 of them are primary CTAs. A3 75% names the same thing from the other side (primaryCta=3/2, 10 disclosures, 0 tabs) - a page that asks for three first actions at once asks for none. This is a design finding on the platform's busiest member page and it wants Ian's eye before anything moves.

analytics E3 50% (the freshness chip reads "Kakakalkula lang - Batay sa iyong logbook", a relative stamp with no absolute time behind it) and R3 67% (one card treatment, four silhouettes across three roles: pill/8px/bar/0px) are ordinary rubric findings on a page that otherwise reads 97%.

dayplanner and ph-intelligence read 100% on their first Filipino walk.

ONE NUMBER I DID NOT BANK AS A DEFECT, ON PURPOSE. analytics N1 scored 75% on "label coverage 1/2, data-i=36, 9 stamped". Nine of thirty-six looks like a translation hole, and I nearly wrote it up as one. It is not: analytics carries its OWN Filipino dictionary under its OWN global (window._anFIL, 31 keys) and applies it itself, so the shared swapper's stamp count cannot see most of what the page translates. A static pass I wrote to generalise this reported 241 unresolvable keys platform-wide and was wrong for exactly the same reason - it knew WH_FIL_COMMON and i18n/pages/<stem>.fil.json but not the page-local globals (_anFIL on analytics, window.WH_FIL on hive at line 1504, _ohApplyI18n's dict on index). An oracle's vocabulary is part of the oracle.

Three keys total, silently English for a Filipino reader. Small, specific, and mechanically certain.

[2026-09-10] RETRACTED and REMOVED (the measurement itself is false): B3 - "community: B3 67% - sentences=13 · >20w=0 · passive=0 · grade>8=2". B3's readability grade is Flesch-Kincaid, whose coefficients are fitted to ENGLISH, and it was applied unchanged to Filipino prose. Measured on the platform's OWN parallel corpus (i18n/*.json holds each English string beside its shipped Filipino): across 193 sentence pairs of 8+ words, the Filipino grades HARDER in 180 of them (93%), mean +4.53 grades, median +4.65; syllables-per-word 1.51 EN vs 1.82 FIL; mean grade 8.7 EN vs 13.3 FIL. 64 pairs PASS in English and FAIL in Filipino, only 2 the other way. The clearest case: "Pick the closest match. You can change scope later." grades 2.3, and its faithful, plain translation "Piliin ang pinakamalapit. Puwede mong baguhin ang scope mamaya." grades 14.1 - the same sentence, +11.8 grades, for being Filipino. Tagalog is agglutinative (naitatala, nagpapalago, disiplinang), so its syllables-per-word runs structurally higher and FK's 11.8 syllable term dominates. These findings measured the LANGUAGE, not the copy, and the platform was being penalised for translating well. The ruler is fixed: Filipino prose is now exempt from GRADE, never from length or voice - the same rule this rubric already applies to standards vocabulary. Only findings that rest ENTIRELY on the grade are withdrawn (no long sentence, no passive voice); English B3 findings stand, because FK is valid for English, and every Filipino finding that also carried a >20-word or passive offence stands on that evidence. [2026-09-10] RETRACTED and REMOVED (the measurement itself is false): E3 - "analytics: E3 50% - chip: "Kakakalkula lang · Batay sa iyong logboo"". E3's freshness vocabulary was ENGLISH-ONLY, so a Filipino page that states its freshness plainly was scored as if it had not. Proven on one page in two languages: analytics reads E3 100% in English on "Saved snapshot, computed 6 min ago · Refresh to recompute" and read 50% in Filipino on "Kakakalkula lang", which is the platform's own shipped translation of "Recomputed just now" - the SAME freshness claim, invisible because the pattern only spoke English. Measured across the dictionaries: 44 English strings carry a freshness word, 25 keep it in Filipino by loanword (snapshot, refresh, generate survive translation) and 19 do not, and those 19 were unreadable to this dim. The ruler is fixed with exactly those measured forms - kalkula/kuwenta (the two verbs Filipino uses for compute), binubuo (built), hiniling (on demand), nakalipas (ago), and the na-/nire- prefixed loanwords the English stems miss because the pattern demands the -d participle. Verified on six cases including the negatives: a chip that names only its SOURCE ("Batay sa iyong logbook", "Based on your logbook") still fails in both languages, so the dim keeps its teeth. Retracted here are ONLY the Filipino findings whose quoted chip the corrected vocabulary now accepts - every one of them a chip that was present and did state its freshness. The Filipino "NO source chip" findings are untouched, because a genuinely missing chip is a real defect in any language, and every English E3 finding stands, because the pattern was always valid for English. This is the fourth English-only vocabulary found in one session, after B3's readability grade, the permission wall and X1's guidance verbs. [2026-09-11] RETRACTED (interpretation only - the measurement stands): R3 - "analytics: R3 67% - cardTreatments=1 · silhouettes=4 for 3 role(s) (pill,8px,bar,0px)". The NUMBER is right and the STORY told about it was wrong. Every note carrying this finding explained it as the four .phase-tab controls falling back to their own 0px corner once the strip wraps at 390. They do not: the parent still has gap:0 and the tabs still have border-radius:0, so R3's joined-group test reads them as ONE BAR at both widths - they were never the fourth silhouette. Re-measured by replicating R3's own roleOf/shapeV against the page root at 390: pill->select(20), 8px->press(12), bar->navigate(4), 0px->press(6). The fourth silhouette is the six .kpi-toggle expanders - Availability, MTBF, MTTR, PM Compliance Rate, Downtime Pareto, Failure Frequency - wearing a square corner while the page's twelve other press controls (refresh-btn, details-toggle, showall-toggle) wear 8px. It is NOT a responsive defect: the toggle is 308px inside a 352px card (87.5%), just under isCardAnatomy's 90% cut-off, and at desktop it crosses that line and is excluded, which is the only reason R3 read 100% at 1280. The inconsistency existed at every width; one width could see it. Fixed by giving .kpi-toggle var(--wh-radius-sm) - the border and tint come from a JS-written inline style that sets no radius, so the class rule wins. Verified at BOTH widths: pill/8px/bar, 3 shapes for 3 roles, 0 collisions, R3 100%, analytics 100%. A mechanism must be measured, not inferred from the one thing that visibly changed.

One in-motion MCP walk, banked onto 6 row(s) that share its cell, page path, language, condition and moment (they differ only in which hive's data sits behind the screens - see tools/critic_walk_groups.py). W3255/W3258/W3261/W3264/W3267/W3270 — Rosa dela Cruz, fleet supervisor of Dela Cruz Delivery Fleet, walks her own six-page arc IN FILIPINO on phone-390: dayplanner -> shift-brain -> community -> analytics -> ph-intelligence -> hive. wh_lang='fil', normal conditions, present moment, mobile+touch. Every survey taken after its own navigation with install:true and recording its own href, so no survey is graded through a page it did not land on. 540 dims graded, 9 sub-100.

THE POINT OF THIS WALK WAS TO SECOND-SOURCE THE i18n CLOBBER FIX, AND IT DID. The founder-console find was a single page: whI18nApply's re-apply overwrote every [data-i] element, including those the application had since computed, so a finished value reverted to its placeholder. The fix stamps what the swap wrote (data-i-applied) and skips any element that no longer holds it. hive.html carries the same shape - _elseLine computes a pointer sentence into a data-i element - so it is the honest second case. Probed as a sequence on the live element: read immediately, then again 5s later, past the 200ms-debounced re-apply. Both reads are byte-identical ("Naghihintay din ng review mo: 2 na shift briefing sa Alert Hub") and clobbered=false, with 27 elements carrying the stamp on that page. The mechanism that erased founder-console's health verdict is now proven inert on a second page that was never touched to make it so.

The same line also settles the double-pluralisation I introduced and then fixed: it reads "2 na shift briefing", not "2 na shift briefings". Composing each countable phrase whole per language is holding.

THE NINE FINDINGS. B3 is the pattern, not an incident: four of the six pages fail it (analytics 33%, community 67%, shift-brain 67%, hive 67%) on the same axis - sentences above grade 8, 1 to 4 per page, with no long sentences and almost no passive voice. The prose is not rambling, it is polysyllabic, and it is being read here by a fleet supervisor in her second language. analytics is the worst at 33% (30 sentences, 1 above grade 8, 2 passive).

hive G3 0% is the sharpest single number in the walk: 24 controls on the board and 3 of them are primary CTAs. A3 75% names the same thing from the other side (primaryCta=3/2, 10 disclosures, 0 tabs) - a page that asks for three first actions at once asks for none. This is a design finding on the platform's busiest member page and it wants Ian's eye before anything moves.

analytics E3 50% (the freshness chip reads "Kakakalkula lang - Batay sa iyong logbook", a relative stamp with no absolute time behind it) and R3 67% (one card treatment, four silhouettes across three roles: pill/8px/bar/0px) are ordinary rubric findings on a page that otherwise reads 97%.

dayplanner and ph-intelligence read 100% on their first Filipino walk.

ONE NUMBER I DID NOT BANK AS A DEFECT, ON PURPOSE. analytics N1 scored 75% on "label coverage 1/2, data-i=36, 9 stamped". Nine of thirty-six looks like a translation hole, and I nearly wrote it up as one. It is not: analytics carries its OWN Filipino dictionary under its OWN global (window._anFIL, 31 keys) and applies it itself, so the shared swapper's stamp count cannot see most of what the page translates. A static pass I wrote to generalise this reported 241 unresolvable keys platform-wide and was wrong for exactly the same reason - it knew WH_FIL_COMMON and i18n/pages/<stem>.fil.json but not the page-local globals (_anFIL on analytics, window.WH_FIL on hive at line 1504, _ohApplyI18n's dict on index). Four dictionary mechanisms, three of them page-local. The count is unproven in either direction until the instrument knows all four; recorded as an open thread, not a finding. An oracle's vocabulary is part of the oracle.

TWO REAL GAPS THE SAME PASS DID FIND, both in the ONE mechanism it models correctly - i18n/pages/<stem>.fil.json is fetched only when a page carries a [data-i^="p_"] key, and two pages carry p_ keys their page dictionary does not define: ai-quality 4 of 6, platform-actions 23 of 24. Three keys total, silently English for a Filipino reader. Small, specific, and mechanically certain.

METHOD: the MCP browser hung for 1800s on analytics (215KB of DOM) after this walk closed and before the coverage thread could be measured live. The walk itself is unaffected - all six surveys were captured before it - and the coverage question moves to the corrected static instrument rather than waiting on the browser. Surveyed: analytics 90 dims, 4 sub-100 | community 90 dims, 1 sub-100 | dayplanner 90 dims, 0 sub-100 | hive 90 dims, 3 sub-100 | ph-intelligence 90 dims, 0 sub-100 | shift-brain 90 dims, 1 sub-100. [2026-09-10] RETRACTED and REMOVED (the measurement itself is false): B3 - "community: B3 67% - sentences=13 · >20w=0 · passive=0 · grade>8=2". B3's readability grade is Flesch-Kincaid, whose coefficients are fitted to ENGLISH, and it was applied unchanged to Filipino prose. Measured on the platform's OWN parallel corpus (i18n/*.json holds each English string beside its shipped Filipino): across 193 sentence pairs of 8+ words, the Filipino grades HARDER in 180 of them (93%), mean +4.53 grades, median +4.65; syllables-per-word 1.51 EN vs 1.82 FIL; mean grade 8.7 EN vs 13.3 FIL. 64 pairs PASS in English and FAIL in Filipino, only 2 the other way. The clearest case: "Pick the closest match. You can change scope later." grades 2.3, and its faithful, plain translation "Piliin ang pinakamalapit. Puwede mong baguhin ang scope mamaya." grades 14.1 - the same sentence, +11.8 grades, for being Filipino. Tagalog is agglutinative (naitatala, nagpapalago, disiplinang), so its syllables-per-word runs structurally higher and FK's 11.8 syllable term dominates. These findings measured the LANGUAGE, not the copy, and the platform was being penalised for translating well. The ruler is fixed: Filipino prose is now exempt from GRADE, never from length or voice - the same rule this rubric already applies to standards vocabulary. Only findings that rest ENTIRELY on the grade are withdrawn (no long sentence, no passive voice); English B3 findings stand, because FK is valid for English, and every Filipino finding that also carried a >20-word or passive offence stands on that evidence. [2026-09-10] RETRACTED and REMOVED (the measurement itself is false): E3 - "analytics: E3 50% - chip: "Kakakalkula lang · Batay sa iyong logboo"". E3's freshness vocabulary was ENGLISH-ONLY, so a Filipino page that states its freshness plainly was scored as if it had not. Proven on one page in two languages: analytics reads E3 100% in English on "Saved snapshot, computed 6 min ago · Refresh to recompute" and read 50% in Filipino on "Kakakalkula lang", which is the platform's own shipped translation of "Recomputed just now" - the SAME freshness claim, invisible because the pattern only spoke English. Measured across the dictionaries: 44 English strings carry a freshness word, 25 keep it in Filipino by loanword (snapshot, refresh, generate survive translation) and 19 do not, and those 19 were unreadable to this dim. The ruler is fixed with exactly those measured forms - kalkula/kuwenta (the two verbs Filipino uses for compute), binubuo (built), hiniling (on demand), nakalipas (ago), and the na-/nire- prefixed loanwords the English stems miss because the pattern demands the -d participle. Verified on six cases including the negatives: a chip that names only its SOURCE ("Batay sa iyong logbook", "Based on your logbook") still fails in both languages, so the dim keeps its teeth. Retracted here are ONLY the Filipino findings whose quoted chip the corrected vocabulary now accepts - every one of them a chip that was present and did state its freshness. The Filipino "NO source chip" findings are untouched, because a genuinely missing chip is a real defect in any language, and every English E3 finding stands, because the pattern was always valid for English. This is the fourth English-only vocabulary found in one session, after B3's readability grade, the permission wall and X1's guidance verbs. [2026-09-11] RETRACTED (interpretation only - the measurement stands): R3 - "analytics: R3 67% - cardTreatments=1 · silhouettes=4 for 3 role(s) (pill,8px,bar,0px)". The NUMBER is right and the STORY told about it was wrong. Every note carrying this finding explained it as the four .phase-tab controls falling back to their own 0px corner once the strip wraps at 390. They do not: the parent still has gap:0 and the tabs still have border-radius:0, so R3's joined-group test reads them as ONE BAR at both widths - they were never the fourth silhouette. Re-measured by replicating R3's own roleOf/shapeV against the page root at 390: pill->select(20), 8px->press(12), bar->navigate(4), 0px->press(6). The fourth silhouette is the six .kpi-toggle expanders - Availability, MTBF, MTTR, PM Compliance Rate, Downtime Pareto, Failure Frequency - wearing a square corner while the page's twelve other press controls (refresh-btn, details-toggle, showall-toggle) wear 8px. It is NOT a responsive defect: the toggle is 308px inside a 352px card (87.5%), just under isCardAnatomy's 90% cut-off, and at desktop it crosses that line and is excluded, which is the only reason R3 read 100% at 1280. The inconsistency existed at every width; one width could see it. Fixed by giving .kpi-toggle var(--wh-radius-sm) - the border and tint come from a JS-written inline style that sets no radius, so the class rule wins. Verified at BOTH widths: pill/8px/bar, 3 shapes for 3 roles, 0 collisions, R3 100%, analytics 100%. A mechanism must be measured, not inferred from the one thing that visibly changed.

B3's readability grade is Flesch-Kincaid, whose coefficients are fitted to ENGLISH, and it was applied unchanged to Filipino prose. Measured on the platform's OWN parallel corpus (i18n/*.json holds each English string beside its shipped Filipino): across 193 sentence pairs of 8+ words, the Filipino grades HARDER in 180 of them (93%), mean +4.53 grades, median +4.65; syllables-per-word 1.51 EN vs 1.82 FIL; mean grade 8.7 EN vs 13.3 FIL. 64 pairs PASS in English and FAIL in Filipino, only 2 the other way. The clearest case: "Pick the closest match. You can change scope later." grades 2.3, and its faithful, plain translation "Piliin ang pinakamalapit. Puwede mong baguhin ang scope mamaya." grades 14.1 - the same sentence, +11.8 grades, for being Filipino. Tagalog is agglutinative (naitatala, nagpapalago, disiplinang), so its syllables-per-word runs structurally higher and FK's 11.8 syllable term dominates. These findings measured the LANGUAGE, not the copy, and the platform was being penalised for translating well. The ruler is fixed: Filipino prose is now exempt from GRADE, never from length or voice - the same rule this rubric already applies to standards vocabulary. Only findings that rest ENTIRELY on the grade are withdrawn (no long sentence, no passive voice); English B3 findings stand, because FK is valid for English, and every Filipino finding that also carried a >20-word or passive offence stands on that evidence. The ruler is fixed with exactly those measured forms - kalkula/kuwenta (the two verbs Filipino uses for compute), binubuo (built), hiniling (on demand), nakalipas (ago), and the na-/nire- prefixed loanwords the English stems miss because the pattern demands the -d participle. Verified on six cases including the negatives: a chip that names only its SOURCE ("Batay sa iyong logbook", "Based on your logbook") still fails in both languages, so the dim keeps its teeth. Irehistro muna ang mga asset sa Logbook." That sentence NAMES its recovery path. The decisive test was the same page in the other language: English inventory reads X1 100%, "all 4 conditional states offer a CTA or recovery guidance", on the identical panel whose English is "No assets registered. Register assets in the Logbook first." Same page, same panel, one difference - the language. The ruler held `i-save` and `simulan` but not `irehistro`, exactly as it had lacked `magsimula` the time before.

Hand-adding one verb per walk cannot converge: Filipino builds imperatives by affix, so the list is always one verb behind the copy, and this was the THIRD widening. So the vocabulary is now DERIVED from the platform's own parallel corpus by a new tool, tools/derive_fil_guidance_vocab.py: i18n/*.json pairs each English string with its shipped Filipino, so wherever the ENGLISH side carries a guidance verb the FILIPINO side IS guidance by construction. 152 such pairs yielded the tokens, each traceable to the sentence that produced it - `irehistro` comes from inventory.json's own "No assets registered. THIS IS THE CLEAN DEVICE PAIR THE PROGRAM HAS BEEN OWED. Every earlier pair this session was contaminated: the two halves were separated by a ruler change, so B3 and E3 deltas were the INSTRUMENT moving, not the width, and the notes had to say so. This pair was walked minutes apart, same person, same session, same hive, same language, same lens - width was the only variable that changed. The result is as sharp as that design allows: across four pages and 360 dims, EXACTLY ONE dim moves. alert-hub, logbook and dayplanner are dim-for-dim IDENTICAL at both widths.

THE ONE MOVER IS analytics R3: 100% on desktop, 67% on the phone - "cardTreatments=1 · silhouettes=4 for 3 role(s) (pill, 8px, bar, 0px)". This is now the THIRD independent observation of the same effect - the J2 worker pair showed analytics R3 67->100 between the same two widths, the Filipino supervisor desktop walk showed it again, and this pair shows it with no lens change to explain it away. J22, ONE MACHINE'S WHOLE LIFE, walked in FILIPINO as a WORKER: asset-hub -> logbook -> pm-scheduler -> analytics -> hive -> audit-log. Ricardo Morales, ricardomorales@auth.workhiveph.com, single-hive worker in Lucena Pharmaceutical Mfg. - the FOURTH hive this dim set has been read in, and the first time this vertical has been walked in Filipino. wh_lang=fil, documentElement.lang read back as "fil" on all six pages, session verified through getDb().auth.getSession() AND wh_hive_name polled until non-null. Each page graded only after it settled, each lens installed on a FRESH page load with install:true asserted. Both widths walked back to back on ONE lens version.

THE WALK FOUND WHAT THE RUBRIC COULD NOT SEE, AND THE NUMBER NEVER MOVED. asset-hub read 100% before the fix and 100% after it. What carried the defect was the a1_ctas RECEIPT added to the survey return this morning: it printed the page's primary CTA verbatim as "Review 2 pending ->" - English, on a page whose documentElement.lang is fil, on a 168x44 button. A percentage cannot say that; a receipt can. This is the plainest argument yet for receipts over scores.

THE HEADING ASKED THE QUESTION IN FILIPINO AND THE ANSWER CAME BACK IN ENGLISH. asset-hub, inventory, shift-brain and pm-scheduler ship the same "what to do next" block: a heading stamped p_whattodonext_8ce2 ("Ano ang susunod na gagawin") over a paragraph, and a primary button stamped p_takeaction_ee0b ("Kumilos ->"). BOTH TRANSLATIONS ALREADY SHIPPED. Then each page's render overwrote the button's textContent with an English label and set an English paragraph beneath the Filipino heading - 18 CTA labels and 18 advisory sentences across four pages, none wrapped in _t().

WHY EVERY i18n MEASUREMENT WAS BLIND TO IT: they count data-i STAMPS. The stamp was still on the element - only the rendered text had changed - so the orphan census reported 0 orphans on a page carrying an English primary CTA, and the platform gate still lists asset-hub as "covered". A gate's SCOPE is part of what it proves, one layer further in than the shared-chrome case: there the untranslated strings lived outside the scanned pages, here they live INSIDE a scanned page, in its JavaScript.

pm-scheduler IS THE SHARPEST CASE, because its copy QUOTES the controls by name. It said: Tap the "Overdue" chip below. On this reader's screen that chip is labelled "Lampas sa Takda". The total-zero branch said click "Add asset"; the button reads "MAGDAGDAG NG ASSET". A quoted control name that appears nowhere on the reader's screen is worse than an untranslated sentence - it sends someone looking for a thing that is not there. This is the T194 rule (advice must not name a control that does not exist) in its bilingual form: the control exists, under another name, for this person. Every Filipino string now names the card or chip by the label it actually wears - "Ubos na", "Mga pending na part", "Paunang paghahanda ng parts", "Mga Asset na Naghihintay ng Approval".

THE SECOND SHAPE OF THE SAME BLIND SPOT, on hive: the entire Shift Handover panel - heading, description and button - carried NO data-i at all, so it was invisible to the stamp census from the other direction. And the extractor could never have caught the button: tools/i18n_page_dict.py matches only elements whose whole content is a bare text node, which puts every icon-bearing control out of its reach. Stamped through a SPAN around the text, never the button (a data-i on the button replaces its innerHTML and takes the icon with it), plus a new i18n/pages/hive.fil.json. hive's N1 rose 75% -> 100% and dropped off its failing list; A2 50% is now its only finding.

C-AI, ON audit-log: THE GATE WAS NOT A GATE UNTIL THE NETWORK ANSWERED. Its supervisors-only check is correct and reads two values that are already in localStorage - but it sat AFTER an await on db.auth.getUser(), and main-content ships VISIBLE on purpose (Arc L L1: revealing it in JS was a ~0.7 CLS bomb), so the gate can only ever HIDE it. On this loaded host the round trip threw TimeoutError WH_DB_TIMEOUT and a WORKER sat looking at the audit-log chrome, an "I-export sa CSV" button and a skeleton reading "Naglo-load ng audit log..." that never resolves for him. No audit ROW ever renders - every query is RLS-refused - so nothing leaks except the impression that the page is his and merely slow. A cached definite "has a hive AND is not a supervisor" now hides the chrome synchronously before the first await; an unknown role still falls through to the async gate exactly as before. Both paths re-verified: the worker sees main-content display:none at first read with the gate rendered, and the supervisor (Christine Dizon) sees main-content block at first paint with 2,310 characters of log, so the CLS fix is intact.

AND THE INSTRUMENT FAILED TWICE IN ONE WALK, BOTH TIMES MINE. First: my settle rule is "text length steady across three reads", and a page frozen on a skeleton is perfectly steady - so it declared audit-log settled while it was still pre-gate, and banked a false 95% with four invented failing dims (E3, G1, C3, A2) that were measuring a loading page. Second: the hardened rule I wrote to fix that searched innerText for loader WORDS, and analytics' own provenance chip contains "kinukuwenta" - a legitimate sentence, not a loader, which would have stalled every analytics walk from here on. The rule now tests for a VISIBLE LOADER ELEMENT (.loading, .skeleton, [aria-busy=true], [data-loading]), which is exactly what audit-log's stuck state is and what analytics' prose is not. A stuck skeleton is invisible to a length-based settle; the fix is to ask what is on the screen, not how long the text is.

ZERO DEVICE DELTA, THE THIRD FILIPINO PAIR. All six pages read identically at 390 and 1280 - same pct, same failing list, same character count: asset-hub 100, logbook 100, pm-scheduler 100, analytics 100, hive 99, audit-log 100. Three Filipino device pairs now, eighteen pages, and not one dim has moved with width.

WHAT REMAINS, UNCHANGED AND DOCUMENTED: analytics N1 75% is the label-coverage mechanism census (1/6 here), hive A2 50% is the worker-role finding whose block count follows the hive (8 in Lucena, 8 in Manila, 9 in Baguio) and which has never once appeared for a supervisor, and audit-log A1 75% is cta=0 on a gate card, which is what a gate card is.

The three rows differ only in which hive's data sits behind the same screens; this walk observed Lucena Pharmaceutical Mfg. What carried the defect was the a1_ctas RECEIPT added to the survey return this morning: it printed the page's primary CTA verbatim as "Review 2 pending ->" - English, on a page whose documentElement.lang is fil, on a 168x44 button. A percentage cannot say that; a receipt can. This is the plainest argument yet for receipts over scores.

THE HEADING ASKED THE QUESTION IN FILIPINO AND THE ANSWER CAME BACK IN ENGLISH. asset-hub, inventory, shift-brain and pm-scheduler ship the same "what to do next" block: a heading stamped p_whattodonext_8ce2 ("Ano ang susunod na gagawin") over a paragraph, and a primary button stamped p_takeaction_ee0b ("Kumilos ->"). BOTH TRANSLATIONS ALREADY SHIPPED. Then each page's render overwrote the button's textContent with an English label and set an English paragraph beneath the Filipino heading - 18 CTA labels and 18 advisory sentences across four pages, none wrapped in _t().

WHY EVERY i18n MEASUREMENT WAS BLIND TO IT: they count data-i STAMPS. The stamp was still on the element - only the rendered text had changed - so the orphan census reported 0 orphans on a page carrying an English primary CTA, and the platform gate still lists asset-hub as "covered". A gate's SCOPE is part of what it proves, one layer further in than the shared-chrome case: there the untranslated strings lived outside the scanned pages, here they live INSIDE a scanned page, in its JavaScript.

pm-scheduler IS THE SHARPEST CASE, because its copy QUOTES the controls by name. It said: Tap the "Overdue" chip below. On this reader's screen that chip is labelled "Lampas sa Takda". The total-zero branch said click "Add asset"; the button reads "MAGDAGDAG NG ASSET". A quoted control name that appears nowhere on the reader's screen is worse than an untranslated sentence - it sends someone looking for a thing that is not there. This is the T194 rule (advice must not name a control that does not exist) in its bilingual form: the control exists, under another name, for this person. Every Filipino string now names the card or chip by the label it actually wears - "Ubos na", "Mga pending na part", "Paunang paghahanda ng parts", "Mga Asset na Naghihintay ng Approval".

THE SECOND SHAPE OF THE SAME BLIND SPOT, on hive: the entire Shift Handover panel - heading, description and button - carried NO data-i at all, so it was invisible to the stamp census from the other direction. And the extractor could never have caught the button: tools/i18n_page_dict.py matches only elements whose whole content is a bare text node, which puts every icon-bearing control out of its reach. Stamped through a SPAN around the text, never the button (a data-i on the button replaces its innerHTML and takes the icon with it), plus a new i18n/pages/hive.fil.json. hive's N1 rose 75% -> 100% and dropped off its failing list; A2 50% is now its only finding.

C-AI, ON audit-log: THE GATE WAS NOT A GATE UNTIL THE NETWORK ANSWERED. Its supervisors-only check is correct and reads two values that are already in localStorage - but it sat AFTER an await on db.auth.getUser(), and main-content ships VISIBLE on purpose (Arc L L1: revealing it in JS was a ~0.7 CLS bomb), so the gate can only ever HIDE it. On this loaded host the round trip threw TimeoutError WH_DB_TIMEOUT and a WORKER sat looking at the audit-log chrome, an "I-export sa CSV" button and a skeleton reading "Naglo-load ng audit log..." that never resolves for him. No audit ROW ever renders - every query is RLS-refused - so nothing leaks except the impression that the page is his and merely slow. A cached definite "has a hive AND is not a supervisor" now hides the chrome synchronously before the first await; an unknown role still falls through to the async gate exactly as before. Both paths re-verified: the worker sees main-content display:none at first read with the gate rendered, and the supervisor (Christine Dizon) sees main-content block at first paint with 2,310 characters of log, so the CLS fix is intact.

AND THE INSTRUMENT FAILED TWICE IN ONE WALK, BOTH TIMES MINE. First: my settle rule is "text length steady across three reads", and a page frozen on a skeleton is perfectly steady - so it declared audit-log settled while it was still pre-gate, and banked a false 95% with four invented failing dims (E3, G1, C3, A2) that were measuring a loading page. Second: the hardened rule I wrote to fix that searched innerText for loader WORDS, and analytics' own provenance chip contains "kinukuwenta" - a legitimate sentence, not a loader, which would have stalled every analytics walk from here on. The rule now tests for a VISIBLE LOADER ELEMENT (.loading, .skeleton, [aria-busy=true], [data-loading]), which is exactly what audit-log's stuck state is and what analytics' prose is not. A stuck skeleton is invisible to a length-based settle; the fix is to ask what is on the screen, not how long the text is.

THE WALK FOUND WHAT THE RUBRIC COULD NOT SEE, AND THE NUMBER NEVER MOVED. asset-hub read 100% before the fix and 100% after it. What carried the defect was the a1_ctas RECEIPT added to the survey return this morning: it printed the page's primary CTA verbatim as "Review 2 pending ->" - English, on a page whose documentElement.lang is fil, on a 168x44 button. A percentage cannot say that; a receipt can. This is the plainest argument yet for receipts over scores.

THE HEADING ASKED THE QUESTION IN FILIPINO AND THE ANSWER CAME BACK IN ENGLISH. asset-hub, inventory, shift-brain and pm-scheduler ship the same "what to do next" block: a heading stamped p_whattodonext_8ce2 ("Ano ang susunod na gagawin") over a paragraph, and a primary button stamped p_takeaction_ee0b ("Kumilos ->"). BOTH TRANSLATIONS ALREADY SHIPPED. Then each page's render overwrote the button's textContent with an English label and set an English paragraph beneath the Filipino heading - 18 CTA labels and 18 advisory sentences across four pages, none wrapped in _t().

WHY EVERY i18n MEASUREMENT WAS BLIND TO IT: they count data-i STAMPS. The stamp was still on the element - only the rendered text had changed - so the orphan census reported 0 orphans on a page carrying an English primary CTA, and the platform gate still lists asset-hub as "covered". A gate's SCOPE is part of what it proves, one layer further in than the shared-chrome case: there the untranslated strings lived outside the scanned pages, here they live INSIDE a scanned page, in its JavaScript.

pm-scheduler IS THE SHARPEST CASE, because its copy QUOTES the controls by name. It said: Tap the "Overdue" chip below. On this reader's screen that chip is labelled "Lampas sa Takda". The total-zero branch said click "Add asset"; the button reads "MAGDAGDAG NG ASSET". A quoted control name that appears nowhere on the reader's screen is worse than an untranslated sentence - it sends someone looking for a thing that is not there. This is the T194 rule (advice must not name a control that does not exist) in its bilingual form: the control exists, under another name, for this person. Every Filipino string now names the card or chip by the label it actually wears - "Ubos na", "Mga pending na part", "Paunang paghahanda ng parts", "Mga Asset na Naghihintay ng Approval".

THE SECOND SHAPE OF THE SAME BLIND SPOT, on hive: the entire Shift Handover panel - heading, description and button - carried NO data-i at all, so it was invisible to the stamp census from the other direction. And the extractor could never have caught the button: tools/i18n_page_dict.py matches only elements whose whole content is a bare text node, which puts every icon-bearing control out of its reach. Stamped through a SPAN around the text, never the button (a data-i on the button replaces its innerHTML and takes the icon with it), plus a new i18n/pages/hive.fil.json. hive's N1 rose 75% -> 100% and dropped off its failing list; A2 50% is now its only finding.

C-AI, ON audit-log: THE GATE WAS NOT A GATE UNTIL THE NETWORK ANSWERED. Its supervisors-only check is correct and reads two values that are already in localStorage - but it sat AFTER an await on db.auth.getUser(), and main-content ships VISIBLE on purpose (Arc L L1: revealing it in JS was a ~0.7 CLS bomb), so the gate can only ever HIDE it. On this loaded host the round trip threw TimeoutError WH_DB_TIMEOUT and a WORKER sat looking at the audit-log chrome, an "I-export sa CSV" button and a skeleton reading "Naglo-load ng audit log..." that never resolves for him. No audit ROW ever renders - every query is RLS-refused - so nothing leaks except the impression that the page is his and merely slow. A cached definite "has a hive AND is not a supervisor" now hides the chrome synchronously before the first await; an unknown role still falls through to the async gate exactly as before. Both paths re-verified: the worker sees main-content display:none at first read with the gate rendered, and the supervisor (Christine Dizon) sees main-content block at first paint with 2,310 characters of log, so the CLS fix is intact.

AND THE INSTRUMENT FAILED TWICE IN ONE WALK, BOTH TIMES MINE. First: my settle rule is "text length steady across three reads", and a page frozen on a skeleton is perfectly steady - so it declared audit-log settled while it was still pre-gate, and banked a false 95% with four invented failing dims (E3, G1, C3, A2) that were measuring a loading page. Second: the hardened rule I wrote to fix that searched innerText for loader WORDS, and analytics' own provenance chip contains "kinukuwenta" - a legitimate sentence, not a loader, which would have stalled every analytics walk from here on. The rule now tests for a VISIBLE LOADER ELEMENT (.loading, .skeleton, [aria-busy=true], [data-loading]), which is exactly what audit-log's stuck state is and what analytics' prose is not. A stuck skeleton is invisible to a length-based settle; the fix is to ask what is on the screen, not how long the text is.

ZERO DEVICE DELTA, THE THIRD FILIPINO PAIR. All six pages read identically at 390 and 1280 - same pct, same failing list, same character count: asset-hub 100, logbook 100, pm-scheduler 100, analytics 100, hive 99, audit-log 100. Three Filipino device pairs now, eighteen pages, and not one dim has moved with width.

WHAT REMAINS, UNCHANGED AND DOCUMENTED: analytics N1 75% is the label-coverage mechanism census (1/6 here), hive A2 50% is the worker-role finding whose block count follows the hive (8 in Lucena, 8 in Manila, 9 in Baguio) and which has never once appeared for a supervisor, and audit-log A1 75% is cta=0 on a gate card, which is what a gate card is.

THE MOST PUBLIC SURFACE ON THE PLATFORM HAD TWO DEFECTS, BOTH ON ALL 54 LEARN ARTICLES.
  * T3 0% - "touch-action:auto, legacy ~300ms click delay + double-tap-zoom not suppressed". Exactly ONE
    of the 54 learn pages set touch-action; the other 53 had been charging every reader a third of a
    second per tap. These pages share no screen stylesheet (learn-print.css is media="print"), which is
    why nothing carried the rule across. Fixed by tools/fix_learn_touch_action.py (53 files, idempotent,
    dry-run first) AND in tools/scaffold_article.py so the 55th article ships correct.
  * C2 97% - the byline ("By WorkHive Editorial Team", the date, "9 min read") at 4.27:1 against the
    4.5:1 that 12px owes. The colour is Tailwind's text-white/45, and this is not a colour-picking
    question: wh-tw.css ALREADY remaps seven low-opacity white utilities away from stock for contrast
    (/45,/50,/55,/60 -> 0.8; /65,/70,/75 -> 0.85). The learn pages load Tailwind from the CDN instead,
    so the app's contrast remediation never reached them - and they use all seven classes (/60 on all
    54 pages, /55 on 53, /45 on 45). Fixed by tools/fix_learn_contrast_remap.py + the scaffold, using
    the platform's own values, body-scoped (0,1,1) so it beats the CDN utility whatever the injection
    order, with NO !important - verified live before the tool was written.
  Re-measured on the walked article: touch-action manipulation, byline rgba(255,255,255,0.8), ZERO C2
  offenders, T3 100%, page 90% -> 92%.

A MEASUREMENT TRAP THAT ALMOST BURIED THE FIRST FIX. After applying the T3 rule the page still read
touch-action:auto and T3 0%, and the file plainly contained the rule. The page was being served by the
SERVICE WORKER from cache: navigating with ignoreCache bypasses the HTTP cache, NOT the SW. Proven rather
than guessed - navigator.serviceWorker.controller was set, a direct fetch of the same URL returned bytes
that DID contain the rule, and the rendered DOM's style blocks did not. Unregistering the SW and clearing
its caches made the fix appear immediately. Recorded because it cuts both ways: a service worker can make
a landed fix look like it failed, and can equally make a stale page look fixed.

THE HISTORIC CALCULATOR i18n BUG IS GENUINELY CLOSED. wh-i18n-lite.js exists because 60 calculator pages
once shipped a complete Filipino dictionary that could never be applied (whI18nApply lived only in
utils.js, which none of them loaded). Measured live here in Filipino: the load-estimation calculator has
8 dictionary keys, 8 data-i elements, and all 8 ARE applied - dictApplied 8 of 8 - at 100% overall.

AN INSTRUMENT FIX, AND IT IS THE SECOND TIME FOR THE SAME REASON. project-manager graded X1 67% on
"Wala pang proyekto: magsimula sa project template sa itaas" - a state that NAMES its recovery path

the same verb in the mag- actor-focus form. Filipino builds imperatives by prefix, so a vocabulary that
lists one form keeps missing the others. Deliberately NOT fixed with a blanket \bmag[a-z]+\b, which would
match "Magandang hapon" and score a GREETING as recovery guidance; the four verbs added are measured from
strings the product ships (magsimula from project-manager's own dictionary, maglagay/magtanong/
magpatuloy from _t() second arguments). Proven behaviourally before and after: the greeting reads

THE CONTENT LAYER IS THE MONOLINGUAL SEAM IN AN OTHERWISE BILINGUAL PLATFORM, and this journey crosses the seam twice. Every page whose own lang declaration says "fil" reads 100%: engineering-design 1,889 chars, project-manager 1,759, project-report 1,482, report-sender 2,109, and the learn HUB 99% at 3,324. THE MOST PUBLIC SURFACE ON THE PLATFORM HAD TWO DEFECTS, BOTH ON ALL 54 LEARN ARTICLES.
  * T3 0% - "touch-action:auto, legacy ~300ms click delay + double-tap-zoom not suppressed". Exactly ONE
    of the 54 learn pages set touch-action; the other 53 had been charging every reader a third of a
    second per tap. These pages share no screen stylesheet (learn-print.css is media="print"), which is
    why nothing carried the rule across. Fixed by tools/fix_learn_touch_action.py (53 files, idempotent,
    dry-run first) AND in tools/scaffold_article.py so the 55th article ships correct.
  * C2 97% - the byline ("By WorkHive Editorial Team", the date, "9 min read") at 4.27:1 against the
    4.5:1 that 12px owes. The colour is Tailwind's text-white/45, and this is not a colour-picking
    question: wh-tw.css ALREADY remaps seven low-opacity white utilities away from stock for contrast
    (/45,/50,/55,/60 -> 0.8; /65,/70,/75 -> 0.85). The learn pages load Tailwind from the CDN instead,
    so the app's contrast remediation never reached them - and they use all seven classes (/60 on all
    54 pages, /55 on 53, /45 on 45). Fixed by tools/fix_learn_contrast_remap.py + the scaffold, using
    the platform's own values, body-scoped (0,1,1) so it beats the CDN utility whatever the injection
    order, with NO !important - verified live before the tool was written.
  Re-measured on the walked article: touch-action manipulation, byline rgba(255,255,255,0.8), ZERO C2
  offenders, T3 100%, page 90% -> 92%.

A MEASUREMENT TRAP THAT ALMOST BURIED THE FIRST FIX. After applying the T3 rule the page still read
touch-action:auto and T3 0%, and the file plainly contained the rule. The page was being served by the
SERVICE WORKER from cache: navigating with ignoreCache bypasses the HTTP cache, NOT the SW. Proven rather
than guessed - navigator.serviceWorker.controller was set, a direct fetch of the same URL returned bytes
that DID contain the rule, and the rendered DOM's style blocks did not. Unregistering the SW and clearing
its caches made the fix appear immediately. Recorded because it cuts both ways: a service worker can make
a landed fix look like it failed, and can equally make a stale page look fixed.

THE HISTORIC CALCULATOR i18n BUG IS GENUINELY CLOSED. wh-i18n-lite.js exists because 60 calculator pages
once shipped a complete Filipino dictionary that could never be applied (whI18nApply lived only in
utils.js, which none of them loaded). Measured live here in Filipino: the load-estimation calculator has
8 dictionary keys, 8 data-i elements, and all 8 ARE applied - dictApplied 8 of 8 - at 100% overall.

AN INSTRUMENT FIX, AND IT IS THE SECOND TIME FOR THE SAME REASON. project-manager graded X1 67% on
"Wala pang proyekto: magsimula sa project template sa itaas" - a state that NAMES its recovery path
("start with the project template above"). X1's Filipino vocabulary held `simulan` but not `magsimula`:
the same verb in the mag- actor-focus form. Filipino builds imperatives by prefix, so a vocabulary that
lists one form keeps missing the others. Deliberately NOT fixed with a blanket \bmag[a-z]+\b, which would
match "Magandang hapon" and score a GREETING as recovery guidance; the four verbs added are measured from
strings the product ships (magsimula from project-manager's own dictionary, maglagay/magtanong/
magpatuloy from _t() second arguments). Proven behaviourally before and after: the greeting reads
false, both real recovery strings read true. project-manager X1 100%, page 99% -> 100%.

THE CONTENT LAYER IS THE MONOLINGUAL SEAM IN AN OTHERWISE BILINGUAL PLATFORM, and this journey crosses the seam twice. Every page whose own lang declaration says "fil" reads 100%: engineering-design 1,889 chars, project-manager 1,759, project-report 1,482, report-sender 2,109, and the learn HUB 99% at 3,324. Every page whose lang says "en" is a learn ARTICLE and reads 89-90% with seven to nine failing dims: ra-11285 90% at 15,867 characters, free-engineering-calculators 89% at 14,873. So the reader's actual path is: a Filipino hub, describing articles in Filipino, that open as fifteen thousand characters of English, and then a Filipino product on the other side. Nothing is broken - there is NO language toggle on the articles, so no control lies to the reader, and documentElement.lang correctly says "en" on the article and "fil" on the hub, which is what a screen reader needs. THE MOST PUBLIC SURFACE ON THE PLATFORM HAD TWO DEFECTS, BOTH ON ALL 54 LEARN ARTICLES.
  * T3 0% - "touch-action:auto, legacy ~300ms click delay + double-tap-zoom not suppressed". Exactly ONE
    of the 54 learn pages set touch-action; the other 53 had been charging every reader a third of a
    second per tap. These pages share no screen stylesheet (learn-print.css is media="print"), which is
    why nothing carried the rule across. Fixed by tools/fix_learn_touch_action.py (53 files, idempotent,
    dry-run first) AND in tools/scaffold_article.py so the 55th article ships correct.
  * C2 97% - the byline ("By WorkHive Editorial Team", the date, "9 min read") at 4.27:1 against the
    4.5:1 that 12px owes. The colour is Tailwind's text-white/45, and this is not a colour-picking
    question: wh-tw.css ALREADY remaps seven low-opacity white utilities away from stock for contrast
    (/45,/50,/55,/60 -> 0.8; /65,/70,/75 -> 0.85). The learn pages load Tailwind from the CDN instead,
    so the app's contrast remediation never reached them - and they use all seven classes (/60 on all
    54 pages, /55 on 53, /45 on 45). Fixed by tools/fix_learn_contrast_remap.py + the scaffold, using
    the platform's own values, body-scoped (0,1,1) so it beats the CDN utility whatever the injection
    order, with NO !important - verified live before the tool was written.
  Re-measured on the walked article: touch-action manipulation, byline rgba(255,255,255,0.8), ZERO C2
  offenders, T3 100%, page 90% -> 92%.

A MEASUREMENT TRAP THAT ALMOST BURIED THE FIRST FIX. After applying the T3 rule the page still read
touch-action:auto and T3 0%, and the file plainly contained the rule. The page was being served by the
SERVICE WORKER from cache: navigating with ignoreCache bypasses the HTTP cache, NOT the SW. Proven rather
than guessed - navigator.serviceWorker.controller was set, a direct fetch of the same URL returned bytes
that DID contain the rule, and the rendered DOM's style blocks did not. Unregistering the SW and clearing
its caches made the fix appear immediately. Recorded because it cuts both ways: a service worker can make
a landed fix look like it failed, and can equally make a stale page look fixed.

THE HISTORIC CALCULATOR i18n BUG IS GENUINELY CLOSED. wh-i18n-lite.js exists because 60 calculator pages
once shipped a complete Filipino dictionary that could never be applied (whI18nApply lived only in
utils.js, which none of them loaded). Measured live here in Filipino: the load-estimation calculator has
8 dictionary keys, 8 data-i elements, and all 8 ARE applied - dictApplied 8 of 8 - at 100% overall.

AN INSTRUMENT FIX, AND IT IS THE SECOND TIME FOR THE SAME REASON. project-manager graded X1 67% on
"Wala pang proyekto: magsimula sa project template sa itaas" - a state that NAMES its recovery path
("start with the project template above"). X1's Filipino vocabulary held `simulan` but not `magsimula`:
the same verb in the mag- actor-focus form. Filipino builds imperatives by prefix, so a vocabulary that
lists one form keeps missing the others. Deliberately NOT fixed with a blanket \bmag[a-z]+\b, which would
match "Magandang hapon" and score a GREETING as recovery guidance; the four verbs added are measured from
strings the product ships (magsimula from project-manager's own dictionary, maglagay/magtanong/
magpatuloy from _t() second arguments). Proven behaviourally before and after: the greeting reads
false, both real recovery strings read true. project-manager X1 100%, page 99% -> 100%.
